title: How to Tell if Your Manager is Actually Good (newsletter.eng-leadership.com), August 17, 2026
author: Ryan Murphy
source: Engineering Leadership newsletter, guest post via Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Guest author Ryan Murphy, writing in Gregor Ojstersek's engineering leadership newsletter, opens with a personal story of a newly promoted manager who told him on his first day 'you are a resource here' and later reneged on an approved training opportunity, using both as concrete illustrations of untrained management in action. He cites a CMI/YouGov study finding 82% of UK workers entering management roles receive no formal management or leadership training, and pairs it with the Journal of Labor Economics paper 'The Value of Bosses,' which found replacing a bottom-decile boss with a top-decile boss raises team output more than adding an entire additional worker to a nine-person team. From there Murphy distills three concrete, observable signals of good management: treating employees as adults judged on outcomes rather than desk-hours, not letting the manager's personal mood define the team's daily atmosphere, and moving past bare feedback delivery into active coaching on how to improve. Each signal is illustrated with a specific negative example (a boss denying a sick day for a cancer screening, a manager whose office culture visibly shifted with their hangovers) that makes the abstract standard concrete and checkable. The piece closes by reframing the entire discussion around training as a systemic gap: most managers are not bad people, they are simply thrown into a high-stakes role with no formal preparation.
points: Cites a CMI/YouGov study finding 82% of UK workers entering management positions receive no formal management or leadership training, framing bad management primarily as a systemic training failure rather than individual character flaws.

Cites the Journal of Labor Economics paper 'The Value of Bosses' (Lazear, Shaw, and Stanton), finding that replacing a bottom-10%-quality boss with a top-10%-quality boss raises team output more than adding an entire extra worker to a nine-person team.

Names 'treats you like an adult' as the first observable good-management signal, illustrated by a boss who denied a junior employee time off to accompany his mother to a cancer screening unless he used a vacation day.

Names 'they are not the atmosphere' as a second signal, describing a workplace where an unpredictable manager's mood swings visibly dictated whether the whole office got pastries and workshops or sat in silence out of fear of being fired.

Distinguishes bare feedback delivery from active coaching as the third signal, arguing good managers close the loop by scheduling live coaching sessions on specific skills rather than considering the job done once feedback is stated.
quotes: On my first day in that job, my manager took me into a meeting room for the usual 'Hey, how are you? Welcome' induction. At the end of that meeting, he said to me, 'Remember, you are a resource here.'

This is the same manager who told me in a 1:1 that I had the green light for some external training course, and then later rescinded that, saying the exact words: 'My promise is worth the paper it's written on.'

According to a study from the Chartered Management Institute (CMI) in partnership with YouGov, 82% of workers in the UK entering management positions have not had any formal management and leadership training.

In the paper titled The Value of Bosses, published in the Journal of Labor Economics, Lazear, Shaw, and Stanton measured that replacing a boss in the bottom 10% of quality with a boss in the top 10% of quality raises the team's total output by more than adding a whole new worker to a team of 9 people.
A way to tell if your manager is actually good is if they don't just look to pass the buck and think that's the job done, but actively help you grow.
